newsitem.title: CHILE: Jury still out on Chile's ground-breaking pension system.
newsitem.headline: Jury still out on Chile's ground-breaking pension system.

text.p: Studied and imitated by government planners around the world it may be, but Chile's all-private pension system nonethless has some of its future beneficiaries unconvinced.
Although the ground-breaking scheme draws praise from economists, Chileans are uncertain about the benefits of the system to which they must by law contribute.
"I had to join a private pension fund...there didn't seem any option," said electrician Manuel Osorio who switched from a state-run fund to the private system in the early 1980s.
All Chilean workers pay 10 percent of their monthly wagechecks into the private pension system which was launched by General Augusto Pinochet's military government in 1981.

Hailed as a revolutionary idea when it was established, the Chilean system has been adopted throughout Latin America and held up by conservatives everywhere as the salvation for creaking state pension schemes.
But unlike Chile, which was able to impose the change with little resistence, other countries do not force savers to contribute to private funds.
The idea of the scheme is simple. Instead of a state authority controlling pensions, savers choose between competing private schemes.

Around $300 million a month pours from payslips into the portfolios of the fund administrators who control nearely $28 billion in assets, equivalent to nearly half the country's gross domestic product.
The system has been credited with giving Chile, Latin America's most successful economy, one of the emerging world's most sophisticated pension markets and a high savings rate.
The country's five million contributors keep track of their savings from regular statements sent by fund managers, known by their Spanish initials as AFPs.
"You can see clearly where your money is. It doesn't disappear into the nation's reserves," said Fernando de Solminihac, general manager of fund administrator AFP Habitat.

Members are free to switch funds and over a million a year do, persuaded by an army of salesmen. Controlling soaring sales costs, which last year came to $180 million, is among the system's biggest headaches.

Fund administrators point to double-digit returns over the past 16 years as evidence that the highly competitive AFPs are much more efficient managers of investments than the traditional state systems.
Despite the much-vaunted returns, lower paid savers like Osorio are concerned about how they will survive on their pensions and wonder whether the private funds really make much difference.
"I'm worried about retiring at 65 as that's when you get sick and my pension won't be enough," said Osorio.
"It seems little different from the previous system. In the end you pay your money and it is all the same."
Investors' confidence took a knock two years ago when the system posted the first bad results in its history, mainly as a result of the poor performance of the Santiago bourse.

Although the AFPs reported positive results last year, they will not in future enjoy the spectacular profits of the 1980s and early 1990s as Chile's economy is maturing with returns on investments slowing, said de Solminihac.
"As the country becomes more mature and developed, rates of return will fall," he said.

Experts' calculations have shown that returns only need to grow an average 4.5 percent a year for the scheme to fulfill its goal of allowing savers to retire on a pension equivalent to 70 percent of their final salary.

Chile's pension system has not been left entirely in the hands of the private sector. The government continues to pay a basic pension, currently a scant $120 month, to those who have not made enough contributions to either a state or private plan to retire on a minimum pension.
Around two million of the five million savers registered with an AFP only pay in from time to time and many of them will end up living on this state pension.
People who have made no contribution to either system receive a tiny state pension, currently $54 a month.
So far just 200,000 AFP savers have retired and the success of the private funds will only be tested around 2020, when workers who joined the system at its startup will begin to draw their pensions.
"We will only be able to judge the AFP system after 40 years when a large number of people retire," said Jorge Norambuena, national director of the state social security agency.
